nepotism

NEP-uh-tiz-um -- from Italian nipote, 'nephew,' from Latin nepos: named for popes who once gave powerful jobs to their own 'nephews.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Nepotism is unfairly favoring relatives or friends with positions of power or advantage.

Voters accused the governor of nepotism after appointing his own daughter to the state's highest-paying advisory position.

Example

Rather than posting the open manager position publicly, the restaurant owner resorted to nepotism, simply handing the job to her college roommate, who had never worked in a kitchen before.

Nepotism means giving power or advantage to relatives or friends instead of the most qualified person -- skipping a public search entirely to hand a management job to an untrained friend is a clear example.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

partiality: Partiality is an unfair leaning toward one side or person, whatever the reason behind it. Nepotism is a specific kind of partiality: the advantage goes to your own relatives, usually in jobs or positions of power. A teacher who always calls on the same student shows partiality; a manager who promotes her own son shows nepotism.

patronage: Patronage is handing out jobs or favors in return for support, especially political support. Nepotism needs no payback at all -- the advantage flows to relatives simply because they are family. A senator rewarding loyal campaign volunteers practices patronage; an owner hiring her nephew practices nepotism.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fairness: equal and just treatment of everyone

meritocracy: a system where advancement is based on ability, not connections

Where it sits · who receives the special treatment — favoritism → nepotism → cronyism

favoritism vs. nepotism: Favoritism is the broad, general word for unfairly preferring anyone, while nepotism specifically names favoritism shown to relatives.

cronyism vs. nepotism: Cronyism is a close cousin of nepotism but focuses on friends and associates rather than family members specifically.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — nepot-

root — nepot-: nephew, grandson (Latin nepos, via Italian nipote)

suffix — -ism

suffix — -ism: a practice, system, or belief (Greek -ismos)

Put it together

Put it together: Nepotism comes from Italian nipote, 'nephew,' from Latin nepos -- the word was coined because certain popes handed powerful church jobs to their own 'nephews,' who were sometimes actually their sons; nepos is also the same root behind the everyday word nephew.

Use the root in a new word: nephew

Use the root in a new word: nephew: Every summer, her nephew visited for two weeks and helped repaint the porch.
